In a statement issued by his spokesperson, Ban deplored the violence and called Sunday on authorities "to urgently initiate a fair process by which those responsible will be brought to justice." Ban also blamed the "tragedy" on a "lack of restraint on all sides." A police official said the death toll from Saturday's violence outside the Presidential Palace in the capital city of Antananarivo had risen to 26. The violence stemmed from an ongoing dispute over who is in charge of the government. Andry Rajoelina, the mayor of Antananarivo, took to the streets one week ago, declaring himself the Indian Ocean island nation's leader after a week of violence and looting that killed at least 80 people and wounded more than 300. Martin said the rally was peaceful in the morning hours of Saturday, until gunshots rang out in the afternoon after the protesters marched from the plaza to the palace. She said it was unclear where the shots were coming from. Some media reports blamed foreign mercenaries for the shootings; others said army guards were responsible or that the army was firing at the mercenaries to protect the crowd. # Madagascar Violence Prompts UN Chief's Call for Reconciliation

United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon has appealed to Madagascar's political rivals to settle their disputes peacefully, following a deadly clash that erupted during an opposition demonstration and claimed the lives of over twenty people.

Following Saturday's chaos near the Presidential Palace, Ban's office released a statement Sunday condemning the bloodshed and demanding that officials swiftly launch an impartial investigation to hold accountable those responsible for the killings. The Secretary-General attributed the disaster to a "failure of restraint among all parties involved" and encouraged every faction to pursue peaceful, democratic solutions guided by responsible governance.

Police reported that the casualty count from the palace-area unrest had climbed to 26 fatalities, with more than 80 people wounded during the protest, according to officials. By the following day, Antananarivo had fallen silent as residents gathered for a memorial honoring those killed.

## Roots of the Conflict

At the heart of the turmoil lies an unresolved power struggle. Andry Rajoelina, who serves as mayor of Antananarivo, took to the streets a week prior and proclaimed himself the rightful leader of the island nation, following a chaotic stretch that had already claimed roughly 80 lives and injured over 300 people amid looting and unrest.

President Marc Ravalomanana responded by dismissing Rajoelina from his mayoral post and installing a replacement.

According to Brittany Martin—an American Harvard Fellow residing in the capital—Rajoelina had organized Saturday's gathering at May 13th Plaza specifically to introduce his newly formed government. She described the morning demonstration as calm, but explained that gunfire erupted in the afternoon once demonstrators marched from the plaza toward the palace grounds. The source of the shooting remained uncertain, with various news outlets offering conflicting explanations—some pointing to foreign mercenaries, others suggesting military personnel opened fire, and still others claiming soldiers were actually shooting at mercenaries to shield the crowd.

## Weeks of Escalating Tension

The unrest traces back to January 26, when demonstrators seized control of government-operated television and radio facilities in the capital. This followed the government's shutdown of a radio station belonging to Rajoelina just hours earlier, mirroring an earlier closure of his television network after it broadcast an interview featuring former President Didier Ratsiraka.

Ravalomanana originally rose to power in 2001 by defeating Ratsiraka in a bitterly disputed election, prompting Ratsiraka's exile to France. Supporters of Ravalomanana now accuse Ratsiraka's relatives of stirring up the current unrest.

Public frustration has intensified partly due to economic disparity—the World Bank estimates the typical Malagasy citizen earns roughly $320 annually—compounded by revelations that Ravalomanana had purchased a presidential jet valued at $60 million.

Rajoelina has called on his followers to demand the president's departure, stating his intention to lead an interim government until a formal transition can be arranged in the nation located off Africa's southeastern shore.

## Diplomatic Response

"Our consistent position has been advocating for dialogue throughout this crisis," noted Rodney Ford, spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy. He added that reports indicated palace security forces had deployed tear gas and fired warning shots into the air in an attempt to scatter the crowd.

*Journalist Dregoire Pourtier reported from Antananarivo, Madagascar, and contributed to this article.*

United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon issued an urgent appeal on Saturday, calling on Madagascar's warring political factions to step back from the brink of further violence and pursue a peaceful resolution to the power struggle that has gripped the Indian Ocean island nation. The statement came in the aftermath of a deadly confrontation near the Presidential Palace in the capital, Antananarivo, where a large opposition rally descended into chaos and bloodshed.

The clash, which erupted as thousands of demonstrators marched toward the seat of government, left at least 26 people dead and more than 80 others injured, according to reports from the scene. Witnesses described a harrowing scene as security forces attempted to disperse the crowd, with gunfire and chaos breaking out amid the tension that has been building for weeks between supporters of President Marc Ravalomanana and those backing his rival, Andry Rajoelina.

Rajoelina, the young and charismatic mayor of Antananarivo, has positioned himself as a self-declared leader challenging Ravalomanana's authority, accusing the president of corruption, mismanagement, and authoritarian tendencies. His supporters have taken to the streets in a series of escalating protests, demanding Ravalomanana's resignation and accusing the government of suppressing dissent. The standoff has plunged Madagascar into its most serious political crisis in years, raising fears of a broader breakdown in order.

In his statement, Ban expressed deep concern over the loss of life and called for a thorough and transparent investigation into the events that led to the deaths. He emphasized that those responsible for the violence—whether security forces, protesters, or political operatives—must be held accountable under the rule of law. "The Secretary-General condemns the violence and calls for restraint on all sides," a UN spokesperson said, relaying Ban's position. "He urges the political leaders of Madagascar to engage in dialogue and find a peaceful, constitutional solution to the current crisis."

The Secretary-General's intervention reflects growing international alarm over the situation in Madagascar, a nation of roughly 20 million people that has struggled with political instability and poverty despite its rich biodiversity and strategic location. Diplomats and regional bodies, including the African Union and the Southern African Development Community, have echoed calls for both Ravalomanana and Rajoelina to prioritize dialogue over confrontation.

Analysts warn that the failure to de-escalate the standoff could plunge the country into deeper turmoil, with the potential for further violence, economic disruption, and a erosion of democratic institutions. **ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar** — Madagascar has been rocked by a wave of political violence in recent days, as tensions between government forces and opposition demonstrators have escalated into deadly confrontations in the capital and other major cities.

## What We Know

According to local officials and humanitarian organizations, clashes broke out following demonstrations linked to disputed political processes and grievances over governance and economic conditions. Security forces reportedly used tear gas and, in some instances, live ammunition to disperse crowds, resulting in a number of injuries and, according to some reports, fatalities. The unrest has prompted businesses to close, disrupted transportation, and raised fears of further destabilization in the Indian Ocean island nation.

Communication blackouts and restricted access to some affected areas have made independent verification of casualty figures difficult, though human rights groups are calling for transparent investigations into the use of force by security personnel.

## International Reaction

The violence has drawn concern from the international community. **United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres** issued a statement through his spokesperson calling for **restraint on all sides** and urging Malagasy authorities to respect human rights and the rule of law.

The Secretary-General emphasized the importance of **dialogue** as the only sustainable path forward, urging both government representatives and opposition figures to engage in "inclusive and peaceful" negotiations to address the underlying grievances driving the unrest. He also called for a full and transparent investigation into reports of violence, particularly any excessive use of force against civilians and protesters.

Guterres reiterated the UN's continued support for Madagascar's democratic institutions and offered UN assistance, if needed, to help facilitate peaceful dialogue between conflicting parties.

## Broader Context

Madagascar has faced repeated political crises over the past two decades, including coups and contested elections, which have compounded chronic poverty and economic instability on the island. Analysts warn that without addressing root causes — including unemployment, corruption allegations, and weak institutional trust — cycles of unrest are likely to continue.

Regional bodies, including the **African Union** and the **Southern African Development Community (SADC)**, are reportedly monitoring the situation closely, with calls growing for international observers to help mediate a resolution.

Efforts at reconciliation, including power-sharing talks brokered by regional and international mediators, have repeatedly stalled, with both sides accusing the other of bad faith.

**Gunfire in the Capital: Antananarivo Reels After Deadly Clash at Presidential Palace**

ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar — The streets around the Ambohitsorohitra presidential palace fell silent Saturday morning, save for the sound of broken glass being swept from the pavement and the low murmur of residents gathering to survey the aftermath of one of the deadliest single incidents in the country's recent political history.

The previous afternoon, thousands of opposition supporters had marched toward the palace grounds, part of a monthslong protest movement demanding the resignation of the sitting president. According to witnesses and hospital officials, the demonstration turned deadly when presidential guards opened fire on the crowd as it approached the compound's perimeter.

"We were singing, we were peaceful," said Voahangy Rasoanaivo, a market vendor who joined the march with her teenage son. "Then there was shooting, and everyone was running over each other. I don't know how my son and I survived. People fell right next to me and did not get up."

Hospital officials in the capital said the toll from the shooting climbed through the night as the wounded arrived in waves. "We received far more casualties than our emergency wards were prepared for," said a physician at one of the city's main hospitals, who asked not to be named because he was not authorized to speak to the press. "Many of the injuries were gunshot wounds to the chest and back, which tells you people were being fired on as they fled, not as they advanced."

Estimates of the dead varied through the weekend, with local officials citing figures near three dozen, while opposition representatives claimed the true number was higher, alleging that some bodies had been removed from the scene before an independent count could be made.

A spokesperson for the presidential guard defended the unit's actions, telling reporters that soldiers had fired warning shots after the crowd attempted to breach a security barrier. "Our forces acted to protect the institution of the presidency from what they assessed to be an imminent incursion," the spokesperson said.
